title: Punnett Squares and Heredity
seo_title: Punnett Square Worksheets: Genotype, Phenotype and Probability (High School Biology)
standard_text: Apply concepts of statistics and probability to explain the variation and distribution of expressed traits in a population.
meta_desc: Free high school biology worksheets on Punnett squares and heredity (NGSS HS-LS3-3): genotype and phenotype probabilities, expected numbers, incomplete dominance, blood types and X-linked traits. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Each parent gives one allele; expected number = total × probability.
body_html:
How to think about it

Each parent gives one allele; a Punnett square shows the chances.

Aa
AAAAa
aAaaa
  • Aa × Aa: 25% AA, 50% Aa, 25% aa → 3 dominant : 1 recessive.
  • Expected number = total × probability. Real counts vary by chance.
  • Other patterns: incomplete dominance (1 : 2 : 1), codominance (AB blood), X-linked traits.
Example

Aa × aa. Chance of aa?

Squares: Aa, Aa, aa, aa

Answer: 50%

Example

Aa × Aa, 200 offspring. About how many aa?

25% of 200

Answer: 50

Common mistakes

  • Saying Aa × Aa gives 50% recessive. It is 25%.
  • Thinking a carrier (Aa) shows a recessive trait.
  • Thinking chances change after earlier births.

faq.q: How do you use a Punnett square?
faq.a: Write one parent's alleles across the top and the other's down the side, fill in each box, then count boxes to find probabilities.

faq.q: What ratio does Aa × Aa give?
faq.a: Genotypes 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, and phenotypes 3 dominant : 1 recessive.

faq.q: Why don't real results match exactly?
faq.a: Each offspring is a chance event. Larger samples usually come closer to the expected ratio.
